Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 91, verses 1–8:

﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ ﴿and by the moon when it follows it﴾ ﴿and by the day when it displays it﴾ ﴿and by the night when it covers it﴾ ﴿and by the heaven and He who built it﴾ ﴿and by the earth and He who spread it out﴾ ﴿and by the soul and He who proportioned it﴾ ﴿and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness﴾.

The oath serves to affirm the report, and what is intended by the emphasis is the implicit warning and threat of annihilation contained in the course of the report.

The waws that come after the pauses (fawasil) are waws of oath.

Each of the sun, the moon, the heaven, the earth, and the soul of man is among the greatest of God's creations in essence and meaning, indicating His wondrous wisdom and mighty power.

Likewise, each of the forenoon (duha), the moon's following of the sun, and the day and the night, is among the most precise of the order which God, exalted is He, has established.

Al-duha (the forenoon) is the time when the sun rises above the horizon of its rising and its rays appear, and it is the time when the sun rises, moving beyond its place of rising by an amount that appears to the observer to be the length of a spear.

He prefaced this by drawing attention to the fact that purifying the soul is the cause of success, and that neglecting its reform is the cause of wickedness and loss.

Al-tuluww (following) means to follow, and what is meant by it is the moon's following the light of the sun at night, i.e., when it appears after the sun has set, as though it follows it in its place; this is a metaphorical following. The moon follows the sun in many states, among them its beginning (istihlal): the crescent appears to observers right after sunset and then remains so for three nights. It also follows the sun when it approaches the stage of ibtidar and when it becomes a full moon (badr). When it becomes a full moon, its following of the sun becomes literal, because it appears when the sun sets, near its setting, before or after it. It also shines during most nights of the month; God made it a substitute for the sun in giving light for a number of nights. For this reason the oath was restricted to the time of its following, because at that time the signs of following appear from it to observers; this time is like the time of the forenoon in the oath by it, so it is as though it were an oath by the time of its following the sun. Thus the oath is accomplished both by the essence of the moon and by its following of the sun.

The verse also indicates that the light of the moon is derived from the light of the sun, i.e., from the directing of the sun's rays to the part of the moon facing the earth, and that it is not luminous by itself. This is a scientific miracle of the Qur'an, and it is among what I pointed out in the tenth introduction.

The sun is mentioned first in keeping with the context, as an allusion to the honouring of Islam, because its guidance, like the light of the sun, leaves no path for misguidance. It also contains an indication of the promise of its spread throughout the world, as the light of the sun spreads over the horizon. The moon is mentioned after it because it gives light in darkness, just as Islam gave light at the beginning of its emergence in the darkness of polytheism. Then the day and the night are mentioned along with it, because they are an example of the clarity of Islam after the misguidance of polytheism; and this is the reverse of what occurs in Surah al-Layl, for reasons that will follow.

The reason for invoking the heaven immediately after the mention of the sun and the moon, and the earth immediately after the mention of the day and the night, is clear. Then the human soul is mentioned, because it is the locus of guidance and misguidance, and this is the intended matter.

The feminine pronoun in His saying "jallaha" (displays it) apparently refers to the sun; so the meaning of the day's displaying the sun is the time of the sun's appearance.

The attribution of displaying to the day is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), and the oath is by the day only because it is a state that indicates the precise order of the terrestrial world. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the earth, i.e., it illuminated the earth so that it was made manifest to observers by the appearance of what is intended, as is said at the falling of rain: "it has sent down" (arsalat), meaning: the sky has sent down its water.

The oath by the day was qualified by the qualifier of the time of its displaying, by way of incorporating the favour into the oath.

The oath began with the sun and its three lights, the original and the reflected; because the sun is the greatest of luminous bodies from which intense light reaches the earth, and because in its condition and the condition of its lights there is an indication that it is an example of the appearance of faith after disbelief and the spreading of piety after wickedness; for disbelief and sins are represented by darkness, and faith and acts of obedience are represented by light. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿He brings them out of the darknesses into the light by His permission﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 16]).

The oath by the day is followed by the oath by the night, because the night is the opposite of the time of day; it is the time of darkness.

Al-ghashy (covering) means concealment. The night does not literally cover the sun; rather, it is caused by the covering of half of the terrestrial globe over the disc of the sun beginning from the time of sunset, and this is the period of that covering; so attributing the covering to the night is a rational metaphor, attributing the act to its time or to its cause (with a fatha on the ba').

The one who truly covers is the rotation of the earth and its turning toward the sun's place of appearance, which is the daily revolution. It has been said that the feminine pronoun in (﴿yaghshaha﴾) refers to the earth, in the same manner as what was said regarding (﴿wal-nahari idha jallaha﴾).

The "idha" in His saying "idha talaha" (when it follows it), His saying "idha jallaha" (when it displays it), and His saying "idha yaghshaha" (when it covers it) is in the accusative position as an adverb of time, attached to a stative predicate that is a circumstance (hal) of the moon, the day, and the night; so it is a stable adverbial phrase, meaning: swearing by each one of these three in the state that indicates its greatest conditions and its most forceful indication of the great handiwork of God, exalted is He.

The building of the heaven is a figure of speech for raising it above the earth by means of building. Al-sama' (the heaven) denotes the horizons of the stars. God, exalted is He, said: (﴿And We have created above you seven paths﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 17]). Restricting the oath by the night to the time of its covering is a reminder of the lesson in the occurrence of the state of darkness after the state of light.

The spreading of the earth (tahw al-ard) is its extension and making it fit for walking, sitting, and lying down. It is said: tahá yatहwu and yatha, tahwan and tahyan, and it is synonymous with "dahá" in Surah al-Nazi'at.

Al-nafs (the soul) is the essence of the human being, as was explained earlier at His saying: (﴿O soul at rest﴾ [al-Fajr: 27]). The indefiniteness of "nafs" (a soul) is for the sense of kind (nau'iyyah), i.e., the species of soul, so it encompasses every soul in a general sense by the indication of context, in the manner of His saying: (﴿A soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾ [al-Infitar: 5]).

The proportioning of the soul (taswiyat al-nafs) is creating it balanced, i.e., not disproportionate in its creation; and it was explained in Surah al-Infitar at His saying: (﴿Who created you and proportioned you﴾ [al-Infitar: 7]).

The "ma" in the three places in His saying "wa ma banaha" (and He who built it), "ma tahaha" (and He who spread it), and "wa ma sawwaha" (and He who proportioned it), is either a verbal ma (masdariyyah), so that the verb after it is interpreted as a verbal noun; then the oath is by matters that are traces of God's power, exalted is He, namely the attributes of action (sifat al-fi'l) of God: His raising the heaven, His spreading the earth, and His proportioning of man.

His saying (﴿fa-alhamaha fujuraha wa taqwaha﴾) is conjoined to (sawwaha), so it is sworn by as well; the verb (alhamaha) is in the sense of a verbal noun, because it is conjoined to the relative clause of the verbal "ma"; and it is conjoined with fa (then) because inspiration arises from the proportioning. The pronoun of the object in (alhamaha) refers to the proportioning, which is the verbal noun taken from (sawwaha). It is also permissible for "ma" to be a relative pronoun referring to the act of God, exalted is He, and the clause (banaha) being the relative clause; i.e., by the building that built the heaven, the spreading that spread the earth, and the proportioning that proportioned the soul.

So the proportioning is achieved from the time of the complete formation of the fetus from the first stages of childhood, since proportioning is the adjusting of the creation and the bringing into being of the bodily and mental faculties; then the quality of the faculties increases, and inspiration results.

Al-ilham (inspiration) is the verbal noun of (alhama), a transitive verb with the hamza, but its unaugmented root is obsolete; and al-ilham is a noun rarely found in Arabic speech, and the lexicographers did not cite any witness for it from Arab speech.

Al-ilham is used in a specific sense for the occurrence of knowledge in the soul without teaching, experience, or reflection; it is knowledge that arises without evidence, whether it is of the kind that is intuitive, such as the inclination toward necessary and intuitive knowledge, or the kind that arises from evidence, such as empirical matters and theoretical rational affairs.

The choice of the verb here is to include all the knowledge of the human being. Al-Raghib said: "Al-ilham: the casting of a thing into the heart (ru'): and this is specific to what comes from God, exalted is He, and from the supreme assembly (al-mala' al-a'la)." Therefore, this word, if it is not one of the Qur'an's innovations, is among what the Qur'an revived; for it is a term of precise significance for inner meanings, and such notions were rarely current in the language before Islam, owing to the scarcity of such meanings occurring in the speech of the Arabs in general. It is derived from al-lahm, which is swallowing at once; it is said: lahima (like fariha). As for applying "ilham" to knowledge that arises in the soul without a basis, this is a technical usage of the Sufis.

The meaning here is: among the effects of the proportioning of the soul is the perception of primary knowledge, and the necessary perception that is graded, beginning with the natural inclination toward beneficial things, such as the infant's seeking the breast the first time, and including the avoidance of harm, such as fleeing from what is disliked, until this reaches the first levels of acquisition through rational reflection; and all of that is inspiration.

The construction of inspiration with wickedness and righteousness in this verse, although God informed people of what is wickedness and what is righteousness through the messengers, is on the basis that, were it not for what God deposited in souls of the perception of knowledge in its various levels, they would not have understood what the divine laws call them to; for without reason it would not be easy for man to understand wickedness and righteousness, and punishment and reward.

The mention of wickedness before righteousness takes into account the circumstances of those addressed in this surah, who are the polytheists, most of whose deeds are wickedness and who have no righteousness; while righteousness is the characteristic of the deeds of the Muslims, who were few at that time.

The verb (alhamaha) appears with the attribution to a masculine pronoun, on the basis that the feminine gender of the verbal noun of proportioning is a non-real feminine, or to observe the wording of "ma" if you take it as a relative pronoun.

The waws that come after the pauses (fawasil) are waws of oath.

Al-duha (the forenoon) is the time when the sun rises above the horizon of its rising and its rays appear, and it is the time when the sun rises, moving beyond its place of rising by an amount that appears to the observer to be the length of a spear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 91, verse 11–13:

﴿Thamud denied (their prophet) in their rebellion.﴾ ﴿When the most wretched of them rose up.﴾ ﴿Then the Messenger of Allah said to them: "The she-camel of Allah, and her drinking-turn!"﴾ ﴿But they denied him and hamstrung her.﴾ [al-Shams: 14].

If the clause (﴿He has succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams: 9])... and so on, is a parenthetical interjection, then this (clause) is the answer to the oath, in consideration of what is consequent upon it in His saying: (﴿So their Lord destroyed them for their sin﴾ [al-Shams: 14]), meaning: truly, that happened because of that. The lam of the answer is omitted for lightening, given the lengthiness of the oath. They have cited this verse as an example of the omission of the lam, and it is similar to His saying, exalted is He: (﴿By the sky containing the constellations﴾ [al-Buruj: 1]) up to His saying: (﴿Destroyed were the people of the trench﴾ [al-Buruj: 4]).

The purpose is an allusive threat to the polytheists who denied the Messenger out of rebellion, which they know within themselves, just as Thamud denied their messenger out of rebellion. This is what requires emphasis by oath, because the polytheists had not perceived that what befell Thamud of annihilation was on account of their denial of the Messenger of Allah sent to them. So Allah alerted them to this, so that they might reflect, or to treat the knowledge of whoever among them knew this as if it were a denial, since their affairs did not follow the requirement of knowledge. It is as if it were said: "I swear that a punishment will surely befall you as it befell Thamud. And indeed the punishment of the sword has befallen the polytheists at the hands of those who opposed them, harmed them and expelled them, and that is more grievous and painful to them."

So the object of (kadhdhabat) is omitted, indicated by His saying after it: (﴿Then the Messenger of Allah said to them﴾), and the estimate is: they denied the Messenger of Allah.

The mention of Thamud and their messenger Salih (peace be upon him) has preceded in Surah al-A'raf.

The bâʾ in (bi-taghwāhā) is causal, meaning: their rebellion was the cause of their denial of the Messenger of Allah sent to them.

al-Taghwa is a verbal noun: one says taghā taghwan and tughyanan. Tughyan is the excess of pride. It has been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He: (﴿And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]) in Surah al-Baqarah. In it there is an allusion to comparing the polytheists of Quraysh in their denial with Thamud, in that the cause of their denial is the rebellion and arrogance against following one whom they do not regard as having any superiority over them (﴿And they said: "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of great standing from the two cities?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 31]).

And (idh) is an adverb of past time, attached to (taghwāhā), because the time of the rising of the most wretched of them to hamstring the she-camel is the time in which the severity of their rebellion became manifest; so they dispatched their most wretched to hamstring the she-camel which had been made a sign for them, and that is the extreme of audacity.

And (inbaʿatha) is the reflexive of baʿatha, so the meaning is: when they dispatched their most wretched, he rose up and undertook it. And (idh) is prefixed to the clause (inbaʿatha ashqāhā).

This adverbial phrase has been placed before its normal position after His saying: (﴿Then the Messenger of Allah said to them: "The she-camel of Allah"﴾), because the rising of the most wretched to hamstring the she-camel is a particular instance of their rebelliousness, and so it is more closely connected to the denial that resulted from the rebellion. In placing it first there is a discharge of the right of this connection, and to convey that the rising of their most wretched to hamstring the she-camel was at their incitement, and it does not escape notice that it happened after the Messenger of Allah had said to them: "The she-camel of Allah." It is also understood from His saying: (﴿but they hamstrung her﴾ [al-Shams: 14]).

(ashqāhā): the most wretched in misfortune. By it is meant a man among them whom the exegetes name Qudar (with a dammah on the qaf and a lightened dal, unpointed) son of Salif, and his being singled out among them in wretchedness is that he was the one who actually committed the crime, even though it was on the counsel of a chieftain among them and at their incitement.

The fa in (fa-qāla lahum rasūlu Allāh) is conjunctive upon (kadhdhabat), so it indicates sequence and immediacy, as is its usual function. The meaning of the speech is: they denied the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so he challenged them with the sign of the she-camel and warned them against harming her and against preventing her from drinking at her turn at the water. It is conjoined to (fa-kadhdhabūhu), meaning: concerning what he warned them of, and they hamstrung her by the denial previously mentioned, which is other than the denial mentioned second. This implies that the sign of the she-camel was sent to them after they had denied, which is the usual course with the signs of messengers, and it is the apparent meaning of what came in Surah Hud.

It is also possible that the fa is for mere mention-order, indicating the conjunction of a detail upon a summary, like His saying: (﴿Then Satan caused them to slip from it, and expelled them from what they were in﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36]), for their slipping is their being removed, which occurs after the expulsion, not before it; and like His saying: (﴿How many a town We destroyed, and Our punishment came upon it﴾ [al-A'raf: 4]).

Thus the meaning is: (﴿Thamud denied in their rebellion, when the most wretched of them rose up﴾). Then this is detailed by His saying: (﴿Then the Messenger of Allah said to them﴾) up to His saying: (﴿but they hamstrung her﴾ [al-Shams: 14]), and the hamstringing occurred at the rising of the most wretched. On this basis there is no necessity to consider the adverbial phrase (﴿when the most wretched of them rose up﴾) as fronted from a delayed position.

The plural pronouns were returned to them in consideration of their being a group, although the pronouns before it took into account that Thamud is the name of a tribe.

(﴿ناقَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ the she-camel of Allah) is in the accusative by way of warning; the estimate is: beware the she-camel of Allah. The intent is a warning against harming her, so the speech is from attaching the ruling to the essences, while the intended meaning is their conditions.

The attribution of (she-camel) to the Name of Majesty is because she was a sign that Allah placed as proof of the truthfulness of the mission of Salih (peace be upon him), and because her emergence for them was contrary to custom.

al-Suqya (the drinking-turn) is a verbal noun of saqa, and it is conjoined to the warning, meaning: beware her drinking, i.e., beware usurping her drinking-turn. The speech is then elliptical with an omitted modifier, or al-suqya is used for the water from which she is given drink, by way of the verbal noun standing for the object, which returns to attributing the ruling to the essence. The intended meaning is a condition known from the context, for the root suqya indicates that the intent is a warning against their watering their camels from the water on the day of her turn.

The denial that follows the warning, His saying: (﴿she-camel of Allah﴾), is a second denial, namely their denial of what the warning entailed of threat and warning of punishment if they did not beware of assaulting that she-camel. This is what is explicitly stated in the verse of Surah al-A'raf in His saying: (﴿And do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you﴾ [al-A'raf: 73]).

With this consideration the expression is correct in contrasting the warning with the denial, although the warning is an performative utterance, since the denial is directed only at what the warning contains of the announcement of punishment.

al-'Aqr: wounding a camel in its forelegs so that it kneels on the ground from the pain, and it is then slaughtered at its throat. Thus 'aqr is a well-known metonymy for nahr (slaughter), since the two are concomitant.

In placing it first there is a discharge of the right of this connection, and to convey that the rising of their most wretched to hamstring the she-camel was at their incitement, and it does not escape notice that it happened after the Messenger of Allah had said to them: "The she-camel of Allah." It is also understood from His saying: (﴿but they hamstrung her﴾ [al-Shams: 14]).

(ashqāhā): the most wretched in misfortune. By it is meant a man among them whom the exegetes name Qudar (with a dammah on the qaf and a lightened dal, unpointed) son of Salif, and his being singled out among them in wretchedness is that he was the one who actually committed the crime, even though it was on the counsel of a chieftain among them and at their incitement.

The fa in (fa-qāla lahum rasūlu Allāh) is conjunctive upon (kadhdhabat), so it indicates sequence and immediacy, as is its usual function. The meaning of the speech is: they denied the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so he challenged them with the sign of the she-camel and warned them against harming her and against preventing her from drinking at her turn at the water. It is conjoined to (fa-kadhdhabūhu), meaning: concerning what he warned them of, and they hamstrung her by the denial previously mentioned, which is other than the denial mentioned second. This implies that the sign of the she-camel was sent to them after they had denied, which is the usual course with the signs of messengers, and it is the apparent meaning of what came in Surah Hud.

It is also possible that the fa is for mere mention-order, indicating the conjunction of a detail upon a summary, like His saying: (﴿Then Satan caused them to slip from it, and expelled them from what they were in﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36]), for their slipping is their being removed, which occurs after the expulsion, not before it; and like His saying: (﴿How many a town We destroyed, and Our punishment came upon it﴾ [al-A'raf: 4]).

Thus the meaning is: (﴿Thamud denied in their rebellion, when the most wretched of them rose up﴾). Then this is detailed by His saying: (﴿Then the Messenger of Allah said to them﴾) up to His saying: (﴿but they hamstrung her﴾ [al-Shams: 14]), and the hamstringing occurred at the rising of the most wretched. On this basis there is no necessity to consider the adverbial phrase (﴿when the most wretched of them rose up﴾) as fronted from a delayed position.

The plural pronouns were returned to them in consideration of their being a group, although the pronouns before it took into account that Thamud is the name of a tribe.

(﴿ناقَةَ اللَّهِ﴾ the she-camel of Allah) is in the accusative by way of warning; the estimate is: beware the she-camel of Allah. The intent is a warning against harming her, so the speech is from attaching the ruling to the essences, while the intended meaning is their conditions.

The attribution of (she-camel) to the Name of Majesty is because she was a sign that Allah placed as proof of the truthfulness of the mission of Salih (peace be upon him), and because her emergence for them was contrary to custom.

al-Suqya (the drinking-turn) is a verbal noun of saqa, and it is conjoined to the warning, meaning: beware her drinking, i.e., beware usurping her drinking-turn. The speech is then elliptical with an omitted modifier, or al-suqya is used for the water from which she is given drink, by way of the verbal noun standing for the object, which returns to attributing the ruling to the essence. The intended meaning is a condition known from the context, for the root suqya indicates that the intent is a warning against their watering their camels from the water on the day of her turn.

The denial that follows the warning, His saying: (﴿she-camel of Allah﴾), is a second denial, namely their denial of what the warning entailed of threat and warning of punishment if they did not beware of assaulting that she-camel. This is what is explicitly stated in the verse of Surah al-A'raf in His saying: (﴿And do not touch her with harm, lest a painful punishment seize you﴾ [al-A'raf: 73]).

With this consideration the expression is correct in contrasting the warning with the denial, although the warning is an performative utterance, since the denial is directed only at what the warning contains of the announcement of punishment.

al-'Aqr: wounding a camel in its forelegs so that it kneels on the ground from the pain, and it is then slaughtered at its throat. Thus 'aqr is a well-known metonymy for nahr (slaughter), since the two are concomitant.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 91, verses 14–15:

﴿So their Lord destroyed them for their sin and leveled them [to the ground]﴾ ﴿and He does not fear its consequence.﴾

That is: their Lord shouted at them with a cry of anger. The meaning of this damdama (the rumbling, the crushing) is the sound of the thunderbolt and the quake by which they were destroyed. He, exalted is He, said: (﴿So the Cry seized them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 41]). The attribution of this to Allah is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because Allah is the Creator of the Cry and its modes. The morphological pattern of (damdama) is fa'lala, and most of the exegetes said: damdama 'alayhim means: He closed the earth over them. One says: dammama 'alayhi al-qabr, when he covered it over. Damdama is an intensive form of dammama, for emphasis, like kabkaba; and accordingly the pattern of damdama is fa'fala.

The phrase (﴿fasawwaha﴾) is a consequence of (﴿damdama 'alayhim﴾): that is, they were equal in their striking of them; so the object pronoun refers to the damdama derived from (﴿damdama 'alayhim﴾).

Those who interpreted (damdama) as "closed the earth over them" said: the meaning of (﴿sawwaha﴾ [al-Shams: 7]) is: He made the earth level over them, so that neither their bodies nor their cities appear in it. They made the feminine pronoun refer to the earth implied by the verb (damdama), and it is like His saying, exalted is He: (﴿If only the earth were leveled over them﴾ [al-Nisa': 42]).

Between (fasawwaha) here and His saying before it, (﴿wa ma sawwaha﴾ [al-Shams: 7]), there is the embellishment of complete paronomasia (jinas tam).

Al-'uqba: what results after an act of the acts, of consequence for its doer or of reward. Since what is mentioned is punishment and overpowering, and it is the custom that the defeated person harbors in himself the seeking of vengeance against his conqueror, so he does not rest until he avenges himself; for this reason they say: "al-tha'r al-munim" (vengeance that keeps one awake), i.e., that which removes sleep from its owner. So whoever overpowers others guards against the defeated being able to take revenge. Allah informed that He is the Victor who is not feared by the one He overpowers to take revenge from Him. This is a kinaya (allusion) to Allah's capacity to punish the polytheists, and that the delay of the punishment from them is a respite for them and not from incapacity. So the clause (﴿and He does not fear its consequence﴾) is a concluding remark (tadhyil) to the speech and an announcement of the ending.

It is permissible that His saying (﴿and He does not fear its consequence﴾) be a simile (tamthil) for their state of annihilation, by the state of one who leaves no one to avenge him; so the simile becomes a kinaya for their destruction root and branch, such that none of them remained.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read (﴿fa-la yakhafu 'uqbaha﴾) with the fa' of conjunction, as a consequence of (﴿fa-damdama 'alayhim rabbuhum﴾). It is written with the fa' in the codices of Medina and the codex of Syria. . . The meaning of the consequence with fa' according to this reading is the consequence of the knowledge of Allah's not fearing them despite their strength, so that by this knowledge their likes among the polytheists may be deterred.

The rest of the ten readers read (﴿wa la yakhafu 'uqbaha﴾) with the waw of conjunction or of circumstance; it is so in the codices of the people of Mecca, Basra and Kufa, and it is the transmission of their reciters. Ibn al-Qasim and Ibn Wahb said: Malik brought out to us a codex of his grandfather, and claimed that he wrote it in the days of 'Uthman ibn 'Affan when he wrote the codices, and in it (﴿wa la yakhafu﴾) is with the waw. This implies that some codices of Medina had the waw, but they did not recite by it, because it contradicted their transmission.
